tagline: The first Iraqi iGEM team: a software platform and home-built bioreactor for turning date-palm waste into bioethanol, built under hard local constraints
summary: Al-Nahrain-IRAQ is the first Iraqi team ever to compete in iGEM, from Al-Nahrain University, with a team drawn from Biotechnology, AI & Robotics Engineering, Civil Engineering and Business Economics. SYNOVA tackles yeast fermentation of date-palm waste into bioethanol, with a software platform of four apps whose governing rule is that a prediction must never be presented as a measurement, so predicted, published-measured and your-own-lab-measured results are kept separate and never combined into one number. The project is defined as much by what Iraq lacks: no local S. cerevisiae collection to borrow, no liquid ethanol sensor purchasable anywhere in Iraq or neighbouring countries at a reasonable price or wait, no local gene bank because of national restrictions, and RT-qPCR primers that took months and arrived only on 19 October. They built the sensor themselves, isolated four candidate wild yeasts from local sourdough, pomegranate vinegar, date vinegar and an overripe date from Najaf, and set an explicit goal of leaving behind protocols, tools and trained people that the next Iraqi team can start from.

dry.frameworks: A hard evidence-provenance rule enforced in code and in every claim: two engines kept separate, with Engine 2 handling measured evidence and Engine 1 handling predicted evidence, and every result labelled predicted, measured (published) or measured (your lab). Pre-registered checks: the team fixed pass criteria before testing and published the failures rather than tuning parameters to pass, writing that 'a model tuned to pass would say less about how it behaves on real batches'. Human Practices used a four-column what-we-heard / who-said-it / what-we-changed / where-it-landed table.
dry.dataviz: Hand-built accessible SVG figures with full text descriptions in <desc> elements, including a three-band dot figure showing the funnel from every testable strain, gene and condition down to the five experiments worth running first at the bench, a two-engine diagram with a dark band separating prediction from measurement, a 74-square grid of environmental samples with four marked as candidate isolates, a four-row prototype-evolution figure, and a load-cell density-sensor explainer.
dry.datascience: Engine 2 is a differential-expression pipeline: RNA-seq results analysed with DESeq2 (PyDESeq2), filtered at padj < 0.05 and at least two-fold change, gene IDs resolved through the R64 reference genome, narrowed across five layers to an 18-gene hand-checked catalogue each with a published effect, covering ethanol, heat, sugar transport and osmotic stress. Its validation check: 83 genes were significant in both of two experiments where about 42 were expected by chance, and MED15 came out at log2 fold change -6.58. Engine 1 is a batch kinetics model plus optimizer whose check failed and was published as failed: it predicted 2.4 g/L ethanol at 13.25 hours where 7.6 g/L was measured, and its grid sweep did not recover the published optimum from Ahmad et al. (2021). The team states that four of Engine 1's parameter values have no published source, that parameters were read from papers with AI assistance and have not yet been re-checked by a team member, that values from Ghose and Tyagi (1979) could not be re-checked at all for lack of full-text access, and that the statistical design of the differential-expression analysis has not been reviewed in depth so its tables should be treated as unreviewed.
dry.software: SYNOVA: four apps behind one landing page. Engine 1 (kinetic model of one batch fermentation plus condition optimizer, which refuses results breaking mass-balance rules), the micro-max method (re-implementation of a published growth-rate method, which matched the published method within a pre-set tolerance and passed a held-out strain), Lab Data (tools where any lab enters its own growth curves, RT-qPCR Ct values, primer and isolate sequences and fermentation runs), and Engine 2 (the differential-expression pipeline). Code on GitLab, data on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.23533297), with a docs/DATA.md listing file sizes and checksums and an honest note that two data files are not yet in the public record and must be requested from a team member. A guided demo was added after stakeholder feedback that the platform had to be usable even by experts. The dry lab also built interactive educational games based on SYNOVA for children. Bioinformatics workflows were built in Galaxy with Trimmomatic, HISAT2 and SAMtools.

good.publicEngagement: The Spirit story is structural, not sentimental: the first Iraqi team in iGEM built a public-engagement programme that ran from primary-school children up to a deputy minister, and documented every rung. School workshops: Ajyal Al-Amal School on 15 July 2026 for 25 children and Sarh Baghdad School on 20 July 2026 for 30 children, 45 minutes each, explicitly designed so children could participate 'regardless of their previous knowledge'. Each session centred on hands-on banana DNA extraction so that a scientific concept became something children could observe directly rather than hear about, supported by interactive games the dry lab built from SYNOVA itself, themed colouring sheets, lab-coat-shaped candies and a question-and-answer competition. Both schools asked the team to return, and the principal of Sarh Baghdad School awarded the team certificates of appreciation. For older audiences they ran two 'AI in Biotechnology' workshops: an online session on 30 July 2026 with the KAUST iGEM team's Synthetic Biology Mentorship Program (13 students, 45 minutes, where Al-Nahrain was hosted as a special guest) and a two-hour session on 30 August 2026 at the American Space inside the American University in Baghdad for 90 participants drawn from students, educators and the wider community. They then convened a public event at Al-Farabi University with two moderated discussion panels, hosted by their supervisor Dr Zaid Nsaif Abbas: 'The AI Revolution: From Data to New Horizons of Innovation' with the AI Research Center at Al-Farabi University, the CEO of First Finance and the Dean of the College of Excellence at the University of Baghdad; and 'From Presence to Impact: Iraq's Voice on the Global Stage', moderated by Dr Muntadher Qasim with an assistant professor from Al-Farabi, a representative of the Office of the Deputy Minister for Scientific Research Affairs and the CEO of Al-Jisr Marketing Company - a panel built squarely around the question of Iraqi participation in global competitions like iGEM, which is the Spirit theme made into a programme. Institutional engagement climbed deliberately: the President of Al-Nahrain University on 28 April 2026, where the team pitched three project ideas to assembled professors and, on the feedback, abandoned all three and started again before arriving at SYNOVA; and Dr Hayder Abdul Zahid, Deputy Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research, together with the syndicate presidents of human medicine and dentistry, on 6 September 2026, to spread the idea of iGEM in Iraq. They also exhibited at ITEX, the Iraqi International Telecommunication and Information Technology Exhibition, talking to technology companies and meeting the President of Al-Imam Al-Sadiq University. Internationally they were visibly a team being helped and then helping back - mentorship from other teams before they started, guest slot in KAUST's mentorship programme, project exchanges with KFUPM and McGill, the KAUST TAWASOL Showcase, and MIT-MAHE's Scents of the World activity where they chose a scent to represent Iraq. Their own stated lesson is unusually clear-eyed: there is no single way to teach science, a hands-on experiment suits a child while open discussion suits university students, 'our responsibility as educators is not just to explain information, but to make it understandable and leave room for curiosity and questions', and they documented their activities and methods specifically so other iGEM teams and educators can adapt them. Accessibility is built into the wiki as a reading-settings panel offering looser spacing (more space between letters, words, lines and paragraphs), narrower lines, a plain background with no grain or glyph field, motion reduction layered on top of the system setting, and high contrast, with settings kept on-device and ignored by printing; every SVG figure carries a written description.
good.ihp: Human Practices was run as an input to design with the change recorded each time. Raghad Al-Shabandar, president of the National AI Center, pointed out that without clear or abundant labelled public data an AI model was the wrong tool and computational and statistical methods would pay off - so the team switched to equation-based models and statistics. Hussain Ali Mohammed, an AI instructor and data scientist, told them their ethanol-yield accuracy was unreliable and pointed them to ODE-based papers, which shaped Engine 1. Abdulrahman Faisal, CEO of Nabu Academy, warned the platform would not be adopted unless it informed labs or industry from their own data - which produced the Lab Data page where any lab enters its own growth curves, Ct values, sequences and fermentation runs. Ahmed Al-Katib, an economic expert and entrepreneurship trainer, said the platform must be as user-friendly as possible even for experts, so they added a guided demo. Muslim Sagban Altamimi, then Head of the Agricultural Engineers Syndicate in Diyala, discussed agricultural production, domestic consumption and spoilage and suggested extending beyond dates to figs and grapes, which went into future work. Dr Mohammed of Al-Khutwat Al-Sareea Company gave them access to his agricultural land to collect raw materials. Deans of Business Economics and Engineering at Al-Nahrain shaped the economic and feasibility thinking, and Manar Al-Obaidi (CEO of First Finance, known from Iraq's Shark Tank) became the team's sponsor after several meetings. The team also completed the two-day iGEM Entrepreneurship Boot Camp and a one-week British Council entrepreneurship programme. Their closing note on all this is refreshingly disciplined: 'We do not consider encouragement alone proof that our scientific design has changed.' They also name the dilemmas they faced - whether to train an AI model or build from published equations, and what to do when a model failed pre-fixed checks - and record choosing the equations and keeping the failures visible.
good.realWorld: The explicit deliverable is infrastructure for the teams that follow: a page titled 'Building the ground for future Iraqi iGEM teams' lists what can be reused - the S. cerevisiae isolate data on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.23533297), SYNOVA's four apps on GitLab, the bioreactor design together with its failure notes, and 22 qPCR primers documented as iGEM Registry parts with their specificity warnings - plus hard-won practical advice (mind the season; start where fermentation is already happening; make your own reference; don't start with ethanol; use enough inoculum for tolerance screening; our media recipes; plan for delays). Because Iraq has no local gene bank, SYNOVA ships a small reference set of yeast genes labs can use to check primers and isolates. The environmental case is date-palm waste valorisation into bioethanol as a substitute for gasoline; the social case is public exposure to bioinformatics, a field the team notes most people locally do not know exists. Content is licensed CC BY 4.0, and AI assistance is disclosed on a Responsible AI section of the Attributions page, including that the PyDESeq2 and SNP-matching Colab code were AI-assisted and that which assistant was used was not recorded.

gemsTakeaway: Build the engagement ladder deliberately and publish your failures: Al-Nahrain went schoolchildren to university students to industry to a deputy minister in one season, each conversation logged as what-we-heard / what-we-changed, and left behind a reuse page (isolates on Zenodo, code on GitLab, Registry primers, bioreactor design with its failure notes, and seven blunt pieces of practical advice) so the next team in their country starts further along than they did.
